metadata.title: Are educated individuals more likely to be civically engaged? Evidence from rural Bangladesh

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Bangladesh Integrated Household Survey (BIHS) pooled across three rounds (2011–12, 2015, 2018–19) and restricts outcomes to a subset of household respondents (one male and one female adult per household) for whom civic engagement questions were asked. The manuscript describes BIHS as nationally representative of rural Bangladesh across eight divisions, but it does not report the use of explicit sampling/analysis weights or any replicate-weight scheme. Because the analysis is conducted with standard regression models (logit, Poisson/negative binomial) and propensity score matching rather than ILSA-style plausible-value achievement scaling, the paper does not specify any PV-weighting or weight-variable application (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT). Analysts should therefore treat the results as based on the available BIHS sample with the authors’ stated restrictions, while noting that complex-survey weighting details are not documented in the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes with plausible values; instead, it models civic engagement indicators constructed from BIHS survey responses (binary yes/no and additive count scores). Because the dependent variables are directly observed survey responses rather than PV-based achievement scales, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap for how incomplete BIHS responses were handled when constructing the analytic sample.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used all three BIHS rounds (2011–12, 2015, 2018–19) and pooled them into a single dataset. Civic engagement outcomes were available only for a subset of respondents: the civic engagement questions were posed to one male adult and one female adult member per household. The final analytic sample size reported for this paper is 24,440. No additional exclusion rules (e.g., missing covariates, outlier trimming) are specified in the provided text.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using BIHS pooled 2011–12/2015/2018–19 data for rural Bangladesh adults, the study leveraged education level (with controls including age, gender, and asset index) to predict an integrated contributions score, finding that higher education is associated with higher overall magnitude of community contributions. This indicates that policies expanding formal education—particularly beyond primary—may generate broader social benefits through increased community investment, while the study’s correlational design and unreported missing-data strategy constrain causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses the Bangladesh Integrated Household Survey (BIHS) pooled across three rural Bangladesh rounds (2011–12, 2015, 2018–19), restricting civic engagement questions to one male and one female adult per household, yielding a final analytic sample of 24,440 adults in Bangladesh. The dependent variables are directly observed civic engagement indicators (binary yes/no items and additive integrated count scores), so plausible values are not applicable. The analysis estimates logit models for binary outcomes and Poisson/negative binomial count models for integrated scores, and it also runs propensity score matching (nearest-neighbor with caliper 0.001) for consecutive education transitions. Across regression results (Table 4), education shows strong positive associations with civic speaking confidence and integrated community leadership/contributions, with reported likelihood increases up to ~31.2 percentage points and integrated score differences up to ~49.3 percentage points. The paper explicitly states the analysis is correlational (no causality), and it does not report a missing-data handling strategy, limiting transparency about how incomplete responses were treated.
